argument: Tolerance is often treated as an unqualified virtue, but taken to its extreme it becomes self-destructive: a fully tolerant society that also tolerates the intolerant lets the intolerant seize power unopposed, which is Karl Popper's paradox of tolerance. Voltaire and the Enlightenment thinkers had to overturn a centuries-old view, going back to Augustine and Aquinas, that intolerance of wrong belief was actually a virtue. The episode argues that everyone is already selectively intolerant (laws are a collective set of intolerances), and proposes a harm-based criterion for deciding when a belief crosses from something to tolerate into something worth actively opposing.
keyIdeas: Tolerance does not mean believing every position is equally correct; it means accepting that other beliefs exist without acting to silence or condemn the people who hold them.

Medieval thinkers justified religious intolerance as compassion using the 'house fire' logic: just as you'd save a friend from a literal burning house, you should intervene to save them from eternal damnation.

Karl Popper's paradox of tolerance: if a tolerant society extends unlimited tolerance even to those working to destroy tolerance, the intolerant will eventually gain power and destroy the tolerant along with tolerance itself.

Laws are a collectively agreed-upon set of intolerances, so even self-described tolerant people already support intolerance toward beliefs like 'murder is acceptable' -- tolerance isn't simply good in every case.

The proposed criterion for when to intervene against a belief is harm to others, not merely to the believer -- which is why most people don't want to outlaw atheism or mainstream Christianity, but do want to outlaw things like murder.

terms.def: Karl Popper's idea that unlimited tolerance, including tolerance of the intolerant, leads to the destruction of tolerance itself.

Protagoras's position that there is no absolute good or bad, only what individual societies or people deem just or unjust -- which runs into a self-undermining problem similar to unrestricted tolerance.
The idea that in a democracy, laws reflect whatever beliefs the majority is willing to be intolerant toward, since public opinion translates directly into legislation.
The medieval justification, from Augustine and Aquinas, that intervening against a friend's damning beliefs is an act of compassion, just as you'd rescue them from a literal burning house.
